faqs.question: What is ammonium bisulphite and what is its application in oilfield water treatment?
faqs.answer: Ammonium bisulphite (ABS, NH₄HSO₃) is an oxygen scavenger used in Oman's oilfield water injection systems to remove dissolved oxygen from injection water before it is pumped into reservoirs. Dissolved oxygen is highly corrosive — even at concentrations of 50–100 ppb, it accelerates pitting corrosion of carbon steel pipelines, flowlines, and injection wellbores, causing premature failure. The reaction is: NH₄HSO₃ + ½O₂ → NH₄HSO₄. Residual ABS concentration in treated water is typically maintained at 5–20 ppm as measured by colorimetric test kits. Ammonium bisulphite is preferred over sodium sulphite for Oman oilfield applications because of its higher reactivity at ambient temperature, lower pH effect, and lower cost per unit of oxygen removed. details.longDescription:

In the oilfield it is a clay stabiliser. Water-sensitive shales and clay-bearing sands swell and slough when they meet fresh water; the ammonium ion exchanges onto the clay surface much as potassium does, holding the clay in place. A 2–4% ammonium chloride brine is the usual non-damaging completion, workover and perforating fluid for such formations, and it is often preferred to potassium chloride where potassium would interfere with downstream analysis or formation-water compatibility. Dissolving ammonium chloride cools the water noticeably, so make brine in batches and allow it to reach ambient temperature before measuring density. The solution is mildly acidic and corrosive to mild steel over time, so add a corrosion inhibitor for long-term packer duty. Keep bags closed and dry; the salt is hygroscopic and cakes in humid coastal air. Ammonium chloride is harmful if swallowed and causes serious eye irritation, and it releases ammonia gas if mixed with caustic or other strong alkalis, so wear goggles and gloves and keep it dry and away from alkalis. title: Bentonite Powder
description: Clay-based drilling mud additive for viscosity control.

details.longDescription:
Bentonite powder is sodium montmorillonite clay (CAS 1302-78-9) milled to 200 mesh, supplied by Global Chemicals LLC in API 13A drilling grade and a technical grade, in 25 kg bags and 1,000 kg big bags from stock in Muscat. The API grade is tested to the API 13A method: a viscometer dial reading of at least 30 at 600 rpm, a filtrate of 15 mL or less in 30 minutes, moisture below 12% and a fine particle size, so a drilling fluid built on it gives predictable viscosity, gel strength and filter cake from the first batch.

In water-based drilling mud, bentonite does four jobs. It builds viscosity and gel strength so the mud suspends drill cuttings and carries them to surface and holds weighting material when circulation stops. It forms a thin, low-permeability filter cake on permeable formations that limits fluid loss and supports the borehole wall. It lubricates and cools the bit, and it provides the base to which polymers, lignosulphonates and weighting agents are added. Spud muds typically run 50–70 kg of bentonite per cubic metre of fresh water; prehydrate the clay in fresh water for several hours before adding salt or other chemicals, because bentonite yields poorly in saline or hard water, and add soda ash to treat out calcium first.

Beyond the oilfield, the same clay is the slurry for diaphragm walls, bored piles and horizontal directional drilling, the grout for sealing boreholes and monitoring wells, and the liner material for ponds, lagoons and landfills, where its swelling on contact with water closes the pores of the soil. Geotechnical and water-well drillers use it at lower concentrations for the same filter-cake effect.

Bentonite is not classified as dangerous goods, but its dust can contain respirable crystalline silica, so wear a dust mask when mixing. Keep bags dry and off the ground, because wet clay swells in the bag and will not disperse. Every lot carries a certificate of analysis to the API 13A tests and a safety data sheet. Handling and storage: borax is low in acute toxicity but is classified as toxic for reproduction in the European Union, so avoid ingestion and dust, wear gloves, goggles and a dust mask, and keep it out of food and children's products. title: Diesel Exhaust Fluid
description: Emission control solution for diesel engines.

details.longDescription:
Diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue, AUS 32) is a solution of 32.5% ± 0.5% high-purity urea (CAS 57-13-6) in demineralised water, made to ISO 22241, the specification every SCR engine maker refers to. Global Chemicals LLC supplies it from stock in Muscat in 10 L and 20 L containers, 200 L drums, 1,000 L IBCs and bulk, to fleet operators, oilfield and drilling contractors, construction, mining, power-generation and marine users across Oman.

What it does. Engines with selective catalytic reduction (SCR) inject DEF into the hot exhaust ahead of a catalyst; the urea breaks down to ammonia, which converts nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water and cuts NOx emissions by up to about 90%. Euro 6 trucks, US EPA 2010 on-road engines and Tier 4 off-road machines depend on it, and a vehicle that runs out or is filled with the wrong fluid will lose power and log a fault. Consumption is roughly 3–5% of diesel burned, so a truck using 300 litres of diesel a week needs about 9–15 litres of DEF.

Why the specification matters. The 32.5% concentration is the eutectic: it gives the lowest freezing point of any urea solution, about −11 °C, and both weaker and stronger solutions freeze at higher temperatures. ISO 22241 also caps biuret at 0.3% and aldehydes, phosphate and metals such as calcium, iron, copper and sodium at parts-per-million levels, because those poison the SCR catalyst or block the dosing injector. Fertilizer urea dissolved in tap water does not meet it and damages SCR systems; never dilute DEF or top it up with water.

Storage and handling in a hot climate: DEF slowly hydrolyses above about 30 °C, releasing ammonia and losing strength, and ISO 22241-3 gives its minimum shelf life as about 18 months at 25 °C, 12 months at 30 °C and 6 months at 35 °C; above 35 °C each batch should be tested before use. Store it indoors or in the shade, in closed HDPE or stainless containers only, never in mild steel, copper, brass or aluminium, which it corrodes and which contaminate it. Use dedicated funnels and pumps. It is non-flammable and low in hazard; rinse spills with water, as it dries to white urea crystals. Every batch carries a certificate of analysis to ISO 22241.

faqs.question: What types of corrosion inhibitors are used in Oman oilfield pipelines?
faqs.answer: Oman's oilfield pipelines experience several types of corrosion requiring different inhibitor chemistries. Sweet corrosion (CO₂-dominated) is the most common in Oman's condensate-rich gas fields — organic film-forming inhibitors (imidazolines, amides, quaternary ammonium compounds) adsorb onto steel surfaces and form a protective hydrophobic barrier against carbonic acid attack. Sour corrosion (H₂S-dominated) occurs in Oman's deep sour gas fields — phosphate ester and film-forming amine inhibitors provide protection, but H₂S also causes hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC) and sulphide stress cracking (SSC) in high-strength steel, requiring inhibitors combined with material selection controls. Galvanic corrosion at dissimilar metal connections is controlled by electrical isolation and material selection, while under-deposit corrosion (UDC) beneath wax, scale, or sludge deposits requires specialised polymeric dispersants combined with film-forming inhibitors. Global Chemicals LLC works with international inhibitor manufacturers to supply formulations for qualification against the operator's own laboratory and field test protocols (e.g. ASTM G170/G185 methods).

faqs.question: How are corrosion inhibitors applied in oil and gas pipelines in Oman?
faqs.answer: Corrosion inhibitors in Oman's oil and gas pipelines are applied by three primary methods: continuous injection (CI) via chemical injection quills installed at wellheads, manifolds, or platform injection points, where inhibitor is dosed proportional to production rate; batch treatment (pigging) where inhibitor solution is pigged through the pipeline as a slug to re-film internal surfaces — used for long tie-back lines or when continuous injection is impractical; and fall-back / squeeze treatment into the formation or tubing for downhole corrosion control. Continuous injection rates are calculated to maintain a minimum effective inhibitor concentration at the most corrosive point in the system (typically highest water cut, lowest temperature, highest CO₂ partial pressure). In operators' pipeline systems, inhibitor injection rates are monitored against corrosion coupons, ER (electrical resistance) probes, and chemical residual analysis to confirm protection. Global Chemicals LLC supplies corrosion inhibitors, with formulation selection supported by its manufacturing partners, for Oman's upstream and midstream operations.

faqs.question: What scale types are found in oilfield equipment in Oman and how are they removed?
faqs.answer: Oman's oil and gas production equipment experiences several distinct scale types depending on reservoir and produced water chemistry. Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) is the most common scale in Oman's carbonate reservoir formations — it deposits in tubing, wellheads, separators, and heat exchangers as produced water pressure drops and CO₂ degasses, shifting equilibrium towards precipitation. It is effectively dissolved by hydrochloric acid (5–15%) or inhibited acid blends. Calcium sulphate (CaSO₄) scale (anhydrite, gypsum) is harder to dissolve and occurs where reservoir brines mix with sulphate-bearing injection water — EDTA or DTPA chelant treatments are required. Barium sulphate (BaSO₄) is the most problematic scale in Oman's commingled production wells — it is nearly insoluble in any standard acid and requires mechanical removal (coiled tubing milling) or inhibition before it forms. Iron sulphide (FeS) scale occurs in sour wells and requires specialised acid dissolvers. Global Chemicals LLC supplies acid and chelant descalants for the carbonate, calcium sulphate and iron sulphide scales above, with application guidance.

faqs.question: What is MDEA and how is it used for gas sweetening in Oman?
faqs.answer: MDEA (methyl diethanolamine) is a tertiary alkanolamine used as the primary solvent in gas sweetening (acid gas removal) units in Oman's oil and gas processing plants. Gas sweetening removes hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) from sour natural gas and associated gas before export, LNG production, or injection. MDEA selectively absorbs H₂S over CO₂ at standard operating conditions (40–60°C, 5–70 bar), making it preferred where H₂S removal is the primary objective and CO₂ slip is acceptable — as in many Omani gas fields. The absorbed H₂S is released by heating the rich MDEA solvent in a regenerator (stripper) at 120–130°C, regenerating lean MDEA for recirculation. MDEA is preferred over MEA (monoethanolamine) because it has lower solvent degradation, lower corrosion rates, lower energy consumption for regeneration, and higher H₂S loading capacity. faqs.question: What is the MDEA concentration typically used in gas sweetening units in Oman?
faqs.answer: In gas sweetening units in Oman, MDEA is typically used at 40–50 wt% aqueous solution concentration, representing the standard operating range balancing absorption capacity, corrosion rate, and solvent viscosity. At concentrations below 35%, absorption capacity is reduced, requiring higher circulation rates and larger equipment. Above 50%, solvent viscosity increases at low temperatures, and corrosion rates accelerate under high H₂S and CO₂ loading. The exact concentration is set during plant design based on gas composition, inlet H₂S content, target outlet specification, and operating pressure. Typical pipeline gas specifications limit H₂S to about 4 ppm and CO₂ to about 2% vol/vol. For plants that need bulk CO₂ removal rather than selective H₂S removal, activated MDEA formulations (typically with piperazine) are used to accelerate CO₂ mass transfer. faqs.question: What is MEG (monoethylene glycol) used for in oil and gas operations in Oman?
faqs.answer: MEG (monoethylene glycol, ethylene glycol) is a primary hydrate inhibitor and gas dehydration chemical used extensively in Oman's oil and gas sector. In subsea and deepwater gas pipelines, hydrates — ice-like crystalline structures of water and gas molecules — can form at high pressure and low temperature, blocking flow lines and creating serious safety hazards. MEG is injected at the wellhead and into pipeline risers to depress the hydrate formation temperature (thermodynamic inhibition), keeping the gas stream in the hydrate-free zone throughout transport. MEG is also used as a dehydration solvent in glycol contactors to remove water vapour from natural gas before export. In Oman's onshore gas fields, MEG injection is standard practice in wet gas gathering systems, condensate lines, and LNG feed gas conditioning. Global Chemicals LLC supplies technical-grade and recovered MEG in bulk and IBC quantities for Oman's oilfield operations.

faqs.question: How does MEG compare to TEG for gas dehydration in Oman oil and gas operations?
faqs.answer: MEG (monoethylene glycol) and TEG (triethylene glycol) are both hygroscopic glycols used for gas dehydration, but they differ significantly in physical properties and applications. TEG has a much higher boiling point (285°C vs MEG's 197°C) and lower vapour pressure, making it superior for deep dehydration in gas processing plants — TEG can achieve dew point depressions of 40–60°C in standard gas-glycol contactors, meeting pipeline water content specifications. MEG is preferred for direct injection into pipelines and wellheads as a flow assurance chemical rather than a bulk dehydration solvent, because its lower molecular weight means lower injection volumes per mole of water removed. In Oman, TEG is the standard dehydration medium in Oman's central gas processing plants, while MEG injection is used in wet gathering lines and multiphase flow lines where TEG contactors are impractical. faqs.question: How is methanol used as a hydrate inhibitor in Oman oil and gas operations?

title: Potassium Chloride
description: Shale inhibitor for water-based drilling fluids.

details.longDescription:
Potassium chloride (KCl, CAS 7447-40-7) in drilling grade is a white crystalline salt at 99% minimum purity, soluble to about 34 g per 100 mL of water at 20 °C, supplied by Global Chemicals LLC in 25 kg and 50 kg bags and bulk from stock in Muscat for drilling, completion and workover contractors across Oman. Why potassium. Shale and clay swell and disperse when they take up water, which causes tight hole, bit balling, sloughing and washouts. The potassium ion is the right size to fit into the clay lattice and its low hydration energy collapses the clay layers, so a potassium-rich mud holds reactive shale in place better than a sodium or calcium mud. Water-based inhibitive muds typically run 3–10% KCl, often with a polymer encapsulator such as PHPA and a glycol or polyamine inhibitor; the exact concentration is set by the shale's reactivity, measured by capillary-suction or hot-rolling dispersion tests. Potassium also reduces torque and drag by keeping cuttings firm and the borehole in gauge.

A 2–7% KCl brine is the standard non-damaging clear fluid for perforating, gravel packing and workover in water-sensitive sandstones, protecting the near-wellbore clays from swelling; saturated KCl brine reaches about 1.16 sg, which sets the density range where it can be used alone. Ammonium chloride is the alternative where potassium would interfere with formation-water analysis or raise gamma-ray log readings. Add KCl after the bentonite is prehydrated and expect some flocculation of it; potassium muds are usually built on polymers rather than on high bentonite contents.

Mixing and handling: KCl dissolves readily but cools the water as it does, so allow brine to reach ambient temperature before checking density. KCl raises the chloride content of the mud, which matters for cuttings disposal and for some formations; check the chloride limits of the waste-management plan. The salt is not hazardous; wear gloves and goggles against dust, and keep bags dry, as it cakes in humid coastal air. description: Indicating desiccant for moisture control.

details.longDescription:
Blue silica gel (CAS 112926-00-8) is self-indicating desiccant: silica gel beads impregnated with cobalt chloride that are deep blue when dry and turn pink as they take up moisture, so the state of a dryer, breather or storage pack can be read at a glance. Global Chemicals LLC supplies it in 2–4 mm, 3–5 mm and 4–8 mm beads, moisture capacity 35–40% by weight, bulk density 0.70–0.75 kg/L, regenerable at 120–180 °C, in 1 kg, 5 kg and 25 kg bags and drums from stock in Muscat.

Where the colour matters. Transformer and switchgear breathers, where the maintenance crew checks the colour on the walk-round; sight-glass cartridges on instrument-air and compressed-air dryers; desiccant pots on gas-sampling lines, analysers and control panels; the small bags that travel with spare parts, electronics and precision instruments; and laboratory desiccators. For bulk gas and air drying where nobody looks at the beads, the white non-indicating gel does the same work at lower cost; for users who want indication without cobalt, the orange gel is the cobalt-free alternative.

Regeneration: spread the pink beads in a shallow tray and heat at 120–180 °C for two to three hours until the blue returns, then cool in a closed container; do not exceed 180 °C, which damages the indicator and the gel structure. Corrosion inhibition. Sodium nitrite is an anodic inhibitor: in the pH 7–10 range it oxidises the steel surface to a thin, tight passive film of ferric oxide that stops oxygen corrosion. It is dosed at 500–2,000 mg/L in closed-loop cooling and chilled-water systems, heat-transfer and glycol circuits, hydrostatic test water, and in the oilfield in packer fluids, completion and workover brines, drilling fluids and pipelines in storage or lay-up. Two rules make it work. First, dose enough: an anodic inhibitor that is under-dosed leaves small unprotected areas that pit faster than bare steel, so the residual is tested and topped up rather than guessed. Second, protect it: nitrite-reducing bacteria eat it, so closed systems carry a biocide alongside it, and chloride and sulphate above a few hundred mg/L raise the dose needed. details.longDescription:
Solvent naphtha for the oilfield (petroleum naphtha; CAS 64742-89-8 for the light aliphatic cut) is a refined distillate with a flash point from −4 °C to 38 °C and an aromatic content that both depend on the cut, and fast evaporation, supplied by Global Chemicals LLC in light, medium and heavy cuts, in 20 L and 200 L drums, 1,000 L IBCs and bulk, from stock in Muscat with deliveries to the interior fields. The general industrial grades for paint and printing are listed under solvents; this page covers the cuts specified by oilfield service companies and operators.

What it does in the field. Naphtha dissolves mineral oil, grease, paraffin wax and light asphaltic residue, and it evaporates without residue, which makes it the cleaning solvent for wellhead and valve maintenance, rig wash, drilling and completion equipment, pumps, pigs, tools and instruments before inspection or re-assembly. Naphtha and naphtha-xylene blends dissolve paraffin wax from tubing, flowlines and tank bottoms where hot oiling is not available, and naphtha is the carrier solvent in paraffin inhibitors, demulsifier and corrosion-inhibitor formulations, diluting the active chemical so it disperses at the injection point. The aromatic content sets solvency: the heavier, more aromatic cut handles wax and asphaltenes, the light cut cleans parts and flashes off fastest.

Handling: naphtha is a flammable liquid (UN 1268, Class 3) with vapour heavier than air that travels to ignition sources and collects in pits, cellars and tanks. Store drums closed and bunded in a shaded, ventilated area away from hot work; earth and bond during transfer; use explosion-proof pumps and non-sparking tools; wear nitrile gloves and goggles; and treat solvent-soaked rags and spent naphtha as flammable waste. Swallowed liquid can enter the lungs and cause severe chemical pneumonitis (aspiration hazard), so never siphon by mouth and do not induce vomiting. Keep exposure within the workplace limit and never use it in a confined space without monitoring and ventilation.

description: Tetrahydrothiophene (THT) odorant for natural gas and fuel-gas leak detection — 208 L drums with CoA, supplied in Oman & GCC.

details.longDescription:
Tetrahydrothiophene (THT, thiolane, C4H8S, CAS 110-01-0) is the odorant that gives natural gas its warning smell. Global Chemicals LLC supplies it at 99.0% minimum purity by GC, 36.4% sulphur, density 1.00 g/cm³, boiling point 121 °C and flash point 13 °C, in sealed 208 L steel drums under a nitrogen blanket, with a batch certificate of analysis, to gas-distribution companies, city-gas projects and industrial fuel-gas operators across Oman and the GCC.

Why THT. Natural gas has no smell, and regulations require it to be detectable by smell at a fraction of the lower flammability limit, typically one fifth. Odorants are either mercaptan blends or THT. THT is chosen for pipeline networks because it resists oxidation, is not lost on the pipe wall to the same degree as mercaptans, and therefore holds a consistent odour intensity along long distribution runs and at the far ends of new networks; its smell is distinctive and does not fade in the pipe. Typical dosing runs at 10–25 mg of THT per cubic metre of gas, set by the regulator's detectability requirement and confirmed by sniff tests or a THT analyser at the network extremities. It is injected by a dosing skid proportional to the gas flow, or by a wick or bypass odoriser on small systems; the oilfield chemicals guide linked on this page covers related products.

Other uses: odorising fuel gas and process gas for leak detection in industrial plants, biogas and syngas before grid injection, and LPG where the specification calls for THT rather than ethyl mercaptan.

Handling: THT is a flammable liquid (UN 2412, Class 3) with an intense, penetrating odour; the smallest spill or vapour release triggers gas-leak reports across a neighbourhood. Keep drums sealed and nitrogen-blanketed until use, transfer with closed, earthed systems into the odoriser tank, store in a ventilated, shaded, bunded area away from ignition sources, and keep a sodium hypochlorite solution ready to oxidise and neutralise spills and contaminated PPE. Wear nitrile gloves, goggles and, for open handling, respiratory protection. Our technical team supplies dosing-skid compatibility information and the GHS safety data sheet.
